mappings.note: The expected answer gives both halves of kath-kuni: local stone and wood keep the house warm (climate and life) and let it flex in mild earthquakes (disaster preparedness). The two narrower items on the same house were split one to each outcome; this one earns both.
Defines Ladakh as a cold desert by temperature and rainfall - a climatic-region classification. Not C-SST1.1, because aridity and cold, not relief, are the criteria.
Silt and mineral deposition by Himalayan rivers building the fertile plain is a landform-formation process. Not C-SST1.2-LO-2, which would need the farming population rather than the deposition.
Flat terrain enabling road and rail is the environment shaping human activity. Not C-SST1.1, because the plain's flatness is a premise, not the thing to be described.
Wind transport and deposition building dunes is explicitly a formation-of-landforms answer. Not C-SST1.2-LO-1, because the desert climate is background, not what is being located.

Argues why water must be conserved in an arid region and gives the taanka as the example - the conservation-sensitivity outcome. Not C-SST1.2-LO-1, because scarcity is assumed and the answer is about saving water.
The Aravallis' role is to hold back the eastward spread of the desert, so the item is about the extent of an arid region. Not C-SST1.1, since the hills' own relief is not what the answer turns on.
Defines a plateau and then describes the Peninsular Plateau - pure identify-and-describe. Not C-SST1.1-LO-2, because its antiquity is mentioned but its uplift is not explained.
Contrast of height and continuity between the two Ghats is a relief comparison. Not C-SST1.2-LO-1, because rainfall contrasts between the coasts are not part of the expected answer.
The eastward flow follows from the plateau's tilt - a description of slope and drainage. Not C-SST1.1-LO-2, because the tilt itself is taken as given rather than explained.

Names plateau tribal communities and asks for their connection to forest and environment, which is the people-and-environment outcome. Not C-SST1.1, because the plateau is only the address of the answer.

Waterfalls valued for tourism, hydropower and irrigation is an argument about what a feature does for the people of a region. Not CG-SST1, which was reserved for items that only name a resource, whereas this one works out the regional benefit.
The delta is defined by the deposition that builds it, and the coast is a follow-on. Formation rather than the bare C-SST1.1, in line with the other delta items.

Identifies Lakshadweep as a 36-island coral archipelago. Not C-SST1.1-LO-1, because LO-1 means classifying rock types in a diagram, and coral is given here as what the islands are rather than as a rock class.
Location of the Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta plus its river-sea-land make-up - landform description. Not C-SST1.3-LO-3, because the mangroves are described, not defended.

Names the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills within the Meghalaya Plateau. Not C-SST1.2-LO-1, because although heavy rainfall is mentioned in the answer, the question asks which hills and what they are known for.
Living root bridges are a human technique grown out of a wet mountain environment. Not C-SST1.1, because a trained root bridge is not a landform.
Asks in general terms how geography shapes lifestyles, culture and economic activity - the interrelationship outcome stated almost verbatim. Not CG-SST1, because the specific LO covers it.

Mountains and seas shaping migration, trade, monsoon and defence is physical setting shaping the life of a people. Not C-SST1.1, because the boundaries are given and their consequences are what must be analysed.

Compares carrying capacity of plains and mountains through soil, climate and ease of movement - environment and settlement. Not C-SST1.1, because the two regions are contrasted for habitability, not described as relief.

Young collision-built Himalayas against ancient eroded Aravallis is a comparison of formation and subsequent denudation. Not C-SST1.1, since both ranges are already named and only their origins are at issue.
Traces silt from Himalayan erosion to the building of the fertile plain - a formation chain. This is the long-answer twin of the short item on the same process, so it carries the same outcome.

Hot desert versus cold desert, both defined by low precipitation - a climatic-region comparison. Not C-SST1.1, because although 'moonland' relief is mentioned the axis of the answer is temperature and rainfall.

Hard ancient rock and an eastward tilt are made to explain both the drainage direction and the waterfalls, which is landform formation by rock and relief. Not the bare C-SST1.1, because the item is causal rather than descriptive.
Short swift rivers forming estuaries against long rivers building deltas - two depositional outcomes. Not C-SST1.1, since the coasts themselves are not what has to be described.

The islands matter for maritime territory, fishing and resource access, which only the goal covers, and for coral-reef biodiversity, which is the conservation LO. No single LO in this frame carries the strategic and resource argument.

Very heavy rainfall makes conventional bridges fail and pushes people to grow root bridges instead - a direct climate-to-practice chain. Not C-SST1.3-LO-1, because swollen streams here are a permanent condition, not a disaster being prepared for.

Explicit map-reading: what the altitude colour scheme lets you infer about the distribution of relief. LO-1 is the frame's only locate-on-a-map outcome, so it takes the map-skill items even though its wording names climatic regions.
The significance argued is endemic biodiversity and the conservation the listing promotes. Not C-SST1.1, because the Ghats' relief plays no part in the answer.

Housing styles across cold mountains, hot deserts and plains are traced to climate and local materials. Not C-SST1.3-LO-1: unlike the narrower kath-kuni item, earthquakes are only one passing clause here and climate carries the answer.
Continuing plate convergence and the resulting rise of the range is formation-in-progress. Not C-SST1.3-LO-1, since seismic risk is not what the question asks about.

Mineral wealth of the plateau and Aravallis supporting mining and industry is the distribution and use of resources, which only the goal states. Not C-SST1.2-LO-2, because climate plays no part in the reasoning.
Food and clothing varying with climate and local produce is the interrelationship outcome in its most literal form. Not C-SST1.2-LO-1, because no region has to be located.

The case asks for a traditional conservation method and how it saves scarce water - the conservation outcome. Not C-SST1.3-LO-1, because chronic scarcity is not a drought event with preventive action, and the taanka is a storage practice.

Part (i) and (iii) turn on which Himalayan belt has the milder climate and richer vegetation (LO-1), while (ii) asks the students to justify using climate and life in the two ranges (LO-2). Neither alone covers the whole item.

Himalayan snowmelt sustaining irrigation and the upstream-dam conflict are environment-and-livelihood (LO-2 of C-SST1.2); the silt enrichment asked in part (ii) is the depositional process of C-SST1.1-LO-2.

Part (iii) asks the learner to weigh large-scale mining against an ecologically important range, which is conservation sensitivity; part (i) rests on the Aravallis' mineral wealth, a resource fact only the goal covers. Not C-SST1.3-LO-2, because the concern raised is habitat and desert-barrier loss rather than pollution.

Part (i) contrasts estuary-forming and delta-forming rivers, a formation question; parts (ii) and (iii) ask about flash floods in the Konkan and delta flooding, which is the flood-hazard side of C-SST1.3-LO-1. Not C-SST1.2-LO-2, because the villages' livelihoods are backdrop and the analysis is of river behaviour and flood risk.
